title: The 8042 keyboard controller's ports and commands
covers: The IBM keyboard controller as the PC defines it: its data and status ports, its command set at port 64h, the keyboard commands sent through port 60h, and the auxiliary-device (PS/2 mouse) commands sent through port 60h. The controller and keyboard commands are those of the Personal System/2 Hardware Interface Technical Reference, the maker's consolidated guide, which lists them all; the auxiliary-device commands come from the PS/2 Mouse Technical Reference, which is not available, so those entries are notes of DOSBox-X with the places searched; the system ports 61h and 62h are not the controller's and are quoted from the list's port file. In this capture's OCR a hex value prints O for 0 and S for 5.

rows.text: The controller presents keyboard data to the system as a byte at data port hex 0060 and may interrupt.
The output buffer is an 8-bit read-only register at hex 0060; a read returns scan codes, auxiliary data or a command's data byte.
The input buffer is write-only at hex 0060 or 0064; a byte written to 0060 goes to the keyboard unless a command expects a data byte.
Data should be written to the input buffer only while the input buffer full bit is 0.
Reading port 60h clears IRQ 1 and IRQ 12, except on a PCjr, and both buffers' changed flags.
A data byte for a pending command is taken as such; a command byte is not sent on but answered by the controller itself.
On a PCjr the byte is stored as the port's data and the call returns.
The byte at port 60h is also set by the buffer transfer, by a PCjr scancode and by the controller reset.
Port 0061 is the keyboard controller's port B, a system control port for compatibility with the 8255; it is read and written at 0061.
Bits 7 pulses an IRQ1 reset, 3 and 2 disable the channel and RAM parity checks, 1 enables speaker data, 0 gates timer 2 to the speaker.
Bits read: 7 RAM parity, 6 channel parity, 5 mirrors timer 2, 4 toggles per refresh, 3 and 2 NMI status, 1 speaker data, 0 timer 2 gate.
The byte is stored; bit 0 sets the timer 2 gate and bits 0 and 1 the speaker, while bits 2, 3 and 7 drive nothing.
A read returns the written low nibble, bit 5 from timer 2 or an off gate, bit 4 a 33 Hz wave, bit 6 a machine flag, bit 7 zero.
On the PC-98 the port C handler writes this byte too, from the latch bit that inhibits the speaker.
Port 0062 is the programmable peripheral interface's data port C on an XT.
Port C bits: 7 RAM parity error, 6 channel parity error, 5 timer 2 out, 4 reserved, 3 and 2 RAM size, 1 coprocessor, 0 loop in POST.
Bits 3 through 0 are a DIL switch's nybble, low or high as port 61h bit 3 selects.
A read returns 0xDF, or 0xFF while timer 2 is high: only bit 5 follows timer 2, every other bit reads 1.
Address hex 0064 is the command/status port: a read returns status, a write is taken as a command.
The status bits: 7 parity error, 6 general time-out, 5 auxiliary output buffer full, 4 inhibit switch, 3 command/data, 2 system flag, 1 input buffer full, 0 output buffer full.
Bit 7 set means the last keyboard byte had even parity; bit 6 set means a transmission timed out.
Bit 5 with bit 0 means auxiliary data in the output buffer; bit 4 is the password state; bit 3 marks a command or data byte.
Bit 2 is the system flag; bit 1 set means the input buffer is full; bit 0 set means the output buffer holds data for the system.
The status byte is 0x1C plus bit 0 from the output buffer's change and bit 5 from the auxiliary buffer's; the other six bits never change.
Bits 7 and 6 are always 0: no parity error or time-out is ever reported.
Bit 5 follows the auxiliary buffer, but bit 4 is always 1 and bit 3 is always 1, a data write to 60h included.
Bit 2 is always 1, so the power-on state is never reported; bit 1 is always 0; bit 0 follows the output buffer.
The reset clears both flags and the buffer transfer sets them; a port 60h read also clears them.
Commands 20h through 3Fh read the controller's internal RAM, the low six bits naming the address; 20h reads address 0, the command byte, to port 0060.
The command byte's bits: 7 reserved, 6 IBM keyboard translate, 5 disable auxiliary device, 4 disable keyboard, 3 reserved, 2 system flag, 1 enable auxiliary interrupt, 0 enable keyboard interrupt.
Commands 90h through 9Fh are accepted and ignored; the case body holds only a TODO for the reset.
Nothing is stored and the output port keeps its value.

rows.text: Command A7h sets bit 5 of the command byte, which disables the auxiliary device interface by driving its clock low.
A disabled interface sends and receives no data.
The command changes nothing: the assignments that would set the flag are commented out.
Command A8h clears bit 5 of the command byte, which releases the auxiliary device interface.
Bit 5 of the command byte is set to 0.
The command is ignored unless the machine's configuration has the auxiliary port enabled.
Command A9h tests the auxiliary device's clock and data lines and places the result in the output buffer.
Bytes 00h-04h: 00 no error, 01-02 a clock line low or high, 03-04 the data line low or high.
Only 00h, the no-error result, is ever returned.
Command AAh makes the controller run its internal diagnostic tests.
Hex 55 is placed in the output buffer if no errors are found.
The controller answers AAh rather than 55h, and marks the keyboard inactive.
Command ABh tests the keyboard's clock and data lines.
The result byte names the fault: 00 no error, 01-04 a keyboard line stuck low or high.
Only 00h is returned, and the keyboard is marked inactive.
Command AEh clears bit 4 of the command byte, releasing the keyboard interface.
Bit 4 of the command byte is cleared to 0.
Command ADh sets bit 4 of the command byte, which disables the keyboard interface by driving its clock low.
A disabled interface sends and receives no data.
Only the flag is stored: commands written to 60h are still answered and host keystrokes still reach the output buffer.
Command C0h makes the controller read its input port into the output buffer; it should be used only with the output buffer empty.
The input port's bits: 7 through 2 reserved; 1 the auxiliary device's data line; 0 the keyboard's data line.
The output buffer receives 40h, a constant, whatever the input port holds.
Command D0h makes the controller read its output port into the output buffer; it should be used only with the output buffer empty.
The value read is the controller's output port.
Bit 0 is always returned set, for programs that read the port and write it back.
Command D1h takes the next byte written to port 0060 as the controller's output port; its bit 0 should not be set to 0.
The output port's bits: 7 keyboard data out, 6 keyboard clock out, 5 IRQ12, 4 IRQ01, 3 auxiliary clock out, 2 auxiliary data out, 1 gate A20, 0 reset.
Bit 1 gates A20; when keyboard resets are allowed, a clear bit 0 restarts the machine; bits 2 through 7 are not kept.
Command D2h writes the next byte from port 0060 into the output buffer as if the keyboard had sent it.
An interrupt occurs if the command byte enables it.
Command D3h writes the next byte from port 0060 into the output buffer as if an auxiliary device had sent it.
An interrupt occurs if the command byte enables it.
Without the auxiliary port configured the command is refused and logged once.
Command D4h sends the next byte written to port 0060 to the auxiliary device.
The next byte written to port 0060 is transmitted to the auxiliary device.
Without the auxiliary port configured the command is refused and logged once.
Command E0h reads the keyboard and auxiliary clock inputs into the output buffer: bit 0 is T0, bit 1 is T1.
The two test inputs are placed in the output buffer as data bits 0 and 1.
The output buffer receives 00h whatever the two clock lines are.
Commands F0h through FFh pulse the output port's bits 0 through 3 low for about six microseconds, a 0 bit naming a pulsed bit.
Pulsing bit 0 resets the system microprocessor.
Nothing is pulsed: a clear bit 0 restarts the machine when keyboard resets are allowed, and bits 1 through 3 do nothing.
Command EDh begins a two-byte sequence whose option byte's bits 2, 1 and 0 select the Caps Lock, Num Lock and Scroll Lock indicators.
The keyboard acknowledges, sets the indicators and continues scanning if it was enabled.
The LED bits are stored and passed to the host's keyboard-LED update, which sets no host indicator: its calls are commented out.
Echo is a diagnostic aid: the keyboard answers it if it was enabled and keeps scanning.
Hex EE is the answer the keyboard sends to an Echo command.
Read ID asks the keyboard for its identification: it acknowledges, stops scanning and sends two ID bytes.
The keyboard ID is two bytes, 83h and ABh, the low byte first.
Set Typematic Rate/Delay makes the keyboard acknowledge, stop scanning, take a rate and delay byte, acknowledge it and continue.
Bits 6 and 5 give a delay of 1 plus their value times 250 ms, within 20%; bits 4 through 0 give the rate; bit 7 is 0.
The delays and rates are two tables of four and thirty-two entries.
Command F4h enables the keyboard: it acknowledges, clears its output buffer and the last typematic key and starts scanning.
Scanning starts, with an acknowledgement sent first.
Command F5h resets all conditions to the power-on defaults: the key types, the typematic rate and delay and the last key.
The keyboard acknowledges, clears its output buffer, stops scanning and awaits instructions.
It acknowledges and stops scanning, but the output buffer is not cleared and no condition is reset.
Command F6h resets all conditions to the power-on defaults.
The keyboard acknowledges, clears its buffer, sets the default key types and rate, and continues scanning.
It acknowledges and keeps scanning, but the output buffer is not cleared and the defaults are not set.
The Reset command starts a program reset and a keyboard internal self-test.
The keyboard acknowledges with ACK and is disabled until the system accepts ACK by raising the clock and data lines.
After acceptance the keyboard reinitializes, performs the BAT and, after its completion code, defaults to scan-code set 2.
The 0xFA acknowledgement is queued and a 400 ms timer starts at once; nothing waits for the host to accept ACK, and writes are ignored until it fires.
The timer sends 0xAA and 0x00, and the reinitialized keyboard's scan-code set is 1 rather than 2.
A 0xFF sent to the auxiliary device resets the mouse: it replies 0xFA 0xAA 0x00, sets the rate to 80 and resolution to 1, and clears reporting and scaling.
Command 0xEC is the auxiliary device's reset wrap mode.
The byte is acknowledged with 0xFA and the mouse's mode is stored as remote.

rows.text: Command 0xEB is the auxiliary device's read data.
Read data is acknowledged with 0xFA; a packet is queued only when reporting and stream mode are both on, and it carries the current button state.

The byte is acknowledged with 0xFA and the mouse's mode is stored as stream.

rows.text: Command 0xE9 is the auxiliary device's status request.
It is acknowledged with 0xFA, and then three bytes follow: the device status, the resolution and the sample rate; the status byte holds the remote-mode, reporting, scaling and button bits.

rows.text: Command 0xE8 is the auxiliary device's set resolution.
It is acknowledged with 0xFA and takes the next byte, whose low two bits replace the stored resolution.
